meta.title: Spaced practice beats cramming
meta.subtitle: A five-minute case for how we schedule training

narrative.throughline: Spacing the same material over time roughly doubles retention versus one long session.
narrative.ask: Move onboarding from one 6-hour day to four 90-minute sessions.

design.motif: faint graph grid + big section numbers

slides.speakerNotes: We schedule onboarding as one long day. The evidence says that is close to the worst way to do it. Here is the case for spacing it out.

slides.actionTitle: Half of what we teach on day one is gone by week two.

bullets.text: Forgetting is fastest right after a single massed session.

slides.speakerNotes: Our post-onboarding quiz scores drop by about half within two weeks. That is not a people problem, it is a scheduling problem.

slides.actionTitle: Same hours, spread across four sessions

exhibit.caption: Four 90-minute blocks with recall gaps between them

slides.speakerNotes: The total teaching time is identical. We just break it into four blocks with a gap in between, and start each block by recalling the last one.

exhibit.caption: Illustrative retention, matched total study time

bullets.text: The gap forces effortful recall, which is what fixes memory.

slides.speakerNotes: In matched studies, the spaced group retains roughly twice as much two weeks later. The mechanism is the gap: recalling after you have started to forget is what strengthens the memory.

slides.actionTitle: Four short sessions cost us nothing extra
slides.speakerNotes: The only real cost is four calendar holds instead of one. Everything else is equal or better.

slides.actionTitle: Let us pilot four-session onboarding next cohort.
slides.speakerNotes: I am asking to run the next onboarding cohort as four 90-minute sessions and compare the two-week scores. Low cost, and the evidence says it is worth it.
